nodes.name: Game Development - Level Design
principles: Visual guidance leads the player through space using signifiers, affordances, and signal-to-noise ratio
Critical areas should be information-rich; less critical areas should be simplified or blurred
Use perspective lines to create natural sightlines toward objectives
Rhythm disruption (breaking a pattern) draws attention more effectively than adding detail
Dynamic range in saturation/brightness makes important elements stand out
Spatial transformations (narrow corridor to open space) capture attention
Signifiers should be used sparingly — immersion breaks when players feel they are following arrows rather than making decisions

nodes.name: Game Development - Lighting for Games
principles: Key light establishes the primary illumination direction and mood
Fill light softens shadows from key, controlling contrast ratio
Rim/back light separates subject from background by creating edge highlights
Practical lights (lamps, screens) provide motivated lighting within the scene
Color temperature creates emotional tone: warm (3200K) = safe/comfortable; cool (6500K+) = sterile/dangerous
Dynamic range in lighting (bright highlights against dark shadows) creates drama and visual interest
Light should guide the eye — brightest areas draw attention first

nodes.name: Game Development - Environment Art
principles: Modular design enables building vast worlds from reusable components
PBR materials (Physically Based Rendering) ensure consistent appearance under any lighting
Trim sheets and tiling textures reduce asset count while maintaining visual variety
Scale cues (door frames, handrails, furniture) establish believable proportions
Surface detail hierarchy: macro shapes read at distance, micro details up close
Environmental wear tells history — scorch marks, rust, fading paint suggest past events

nodes.name: Game Development - Visual Storytelling
principles: Every object placement implies intent — what was left behind? What was moved?
Signs of habitation (chairs pushed in, food on table) suggest recent presence
Damage and decay tell temporal stories — fresh vs. ancient environments feel different
Color palettes communicate faction identity and emotional state
Lighting quality reveals narrative tone: harsh = conflict; soft = safety
Environmental clutter density correlates with activity level of the space

nodes.name: Game Development - Game Feel
principles: Juice (screen shake, particles, sound) communicates impact and weight
Feedback must be immediate — player action to response within 100ms feels responsive
Particle effects communicate state changes: hit sparks, shield impacts, explosion debris
Sound design layers frequency bands: low = power/tension; high = alertness/beauty
Camera movement reinforces physics — slow-mo on impact, snap-back to normal
Visual feedback should match audio feedback for cohesive sensory experience

nodes.name: Art School - Color Theory
principles: Warm colors (red, orange, yellow) advance visually; cool colors (blue, green, purple) recede
Complementary color pairs (opposite on wheel) create maximum contrast and visual tension
Analogous colors (adjacent on wheel) create harmony and calm
Color temperature contrast (warm vs. cool) is more emotionally powerful than value contrast alone
Saturation reduction in background elements pushes them back; high saturation pulls forward
Color associations are cultural but some are universal: red=danger/passion, blue=calm/distance, green=nature/safety
A limited palette (3-5 colors) creates cohesion; unlimited palettes feel chaotic

nodes.name: Art School - Composition
principles: Rule of thirds: placing subjects at intersection points creates dynamic balance
Golden ratio (1.618) appears naturally in pleasing compositions — use as guide, not rule
Leading lines draw the eye through the composition toward a focal point
Framing within framing (arches, windows, debris fields) adds depth and focus
Balance can be symmetrical (formal, stable) or asymmetrical (dynamic, interesting)
Negative space is as important as positive space — it gives the eye rest
Triangular composition creates stability; diagonal composition creates tension

nodes.name: Art School - Form and Mass
principles: Silhouette readability determines if a shape reads at distance — test by filling with solid black
Geometric simplicity (box, sphere, cylinder) communicates function clearly
Proportion changes perception: tall=noble/imposing; short=stable/grounded; wide=powerful
Industrial design follows form-function relationship: visible structure implies purpose
Edge variation (hard vs. soft edges) creates visual interest and guides attention
Repetition with variation creates rhythm without monotony
Scale contrast (large small element among small elements) draws immediate attention

nodes.name: Art School - Light and Shadow
principles: Chiaroscuro (strong light-dark contrast) creates drama and volume
Rim lighting separates subjects from background by creating edge definition
Shadow direction establishes light source consistency — inconsistent shadows break believability
Soft shadows = large/diffuse light source; hard shadows = small/distant light source
Light falloff (inverse square law) creates depth perception in 3D space
Cast shadows ground objects to surfaces — floating without shadow feels disconnected
Ambient occlusion at contact points adds weight and realism

nodes.name: Art School - Material Rendering
principles: Roughness controls how light scatters: smooth=specular highlights; rough=diffuse reflection
Metallic property determines if surface reflects environment (metal) or has base color (non-metal)
Surface imperfections sell realism: scratches, fingerprints, wear patterns break up perfect surfaces
Normal maps add micro-detail without geometry cost — essential for game performance
Subsurface scattering makes translucent materials (skin, wax, fabric) feel alive
Material aging follows predictable patterns: rust at edges, fading on exposed surfaces, grime in crevices
PBR workflow ensures materials look consistent under any lighting condition

nodes.name: School_3_Film_School - Cinematography
principles: Camera angle defines power relationship: low angle = subject powerful; high angle = subject vulnerable
Close-up creates intimacy and emotional connection; wide shot establishes context and scale
Dutch angle (tilted camera) creates unease and disorientation
Tracking shots follow action and create immersion; static shots create tension and anticipation
Depth of field isolates subjects - shallow DOF for emotion, deep DOF for environmental storytelling
Camera movement should be motivated by narrative purpose, not decoration

nodes.name: School_3_Film_School - Lighting for Film
principles: Three-point lighting: key (main), fill (soften shadows), rim (separate from background)
Motivated lighting: every light source should have a visible or implied practical source in the scene
High-key lighting (bright, low contrast) = comedy/safety; low-key lighting (dark, high contrast) = drama/tension
Practical lights (lamps, screens, fire) provide both illumination and narrative context
Color temperature shifts between scenes signal emotional transitions

nodes.name: School_3_Film_School - Production Design
principles: Every prop placement tells a story - what was left in hurry vs. careful arrangement
Period accuracy creates believability but should serve the narrative, not constrain it
Color palette consistency across sets establishes visual identity for locations
Scale and proportion communicate function: control panels at waist height, warning lights at eye level
Signs of use (wear patterns, personal items) make spaces feel inhabited rather than staged

nodes.name: School_4_Architecture_School - Spatial Design
principles: Human scale reference: door heights ~2m, ceiling heights 2.4-3.5m for comfort
Circulation paths should be intuitive - main corridors wider than secondary passages
Room size relative to function: intimate spaces <20sqm, gathering spaces >50sqm
Thresholds (doorways, arches) signal transition between spatial experiences
Sight lines through spaces create depth and guide movement naturally

nodes.name: School_4_Architecture_School - Materiality
principles: Material honesty: surfaces should express their true nature - concrete looks like concrete
Texture contrast adds visual interest at human touch distance (0.5-2m from viewer)
Floor materials define function: hard = utilitarian; soft = comfort/rest areas
Wall treatments communicate permanence: metal/concrete = permanent; fabric/wood = temporary

nodes.name: School_4_Architecture_School - Lighting Design
principles: Layered lighting: ambient (general), task (functional), accent (dramatic)
Task lighting focused on work surfaces at 300-500 lux; ambient at 100-200 lux
Accent lighting creates focal points and visual hierarchy within spaces
Natural light simulation through directional sources with warm color temperature

nodes.name: School_5_Engineering_School - Spacecraft Design
principles: Form follows physics: spacecraft shapes driven by aerodynamics (atmosphere) or volume efficiency (space)
Modular design enables repair and replacement - ISS modules bolt together like LEGO
Thermal management dictates external features: radiators, heat shields, reflective surfaces
Radiation shielding adds mass - often water walls or polyethylene composites in real designs
Solar arrays are large flat panels optimized for surface area - primary power source in space
Redundancy is built into critical systems - visible as duplicate components and access panels

nodes.name: School_5_Engineering_School - Industrial Design
principles: Ergonomic controls placed within natural reach zone (arm length, waist to shoulder height)
Control layout follows functional grouping: related functions clustered together
Status indicators at eye level; critical warnings in red/orange with high contrast
Cable management and clean surfaces reduce maintenance complexity and visual clutter

nodes.name: School_6_Unreal_Craft_School - Editor Modes
principles: Modeling Mode enables direct mesh creation and editing within the editor viewport
Mesh Paint Mode allows vertex color painting and material weight adjustment on static meshes
Foliage Mode enables rapid placement of vegetation with density, rotation, and scale variation controls
Viewport camera can be controlled via console commands for precise framing and composition

nodes.name: School_6_Unreal_Craft_School - Console Commands
principles: EditorModeManager ActivateMode command switches editor modes programmatically
ExecuteCommand allows running any Unreal Engine console command from external tools
Set_camera and set_viewport_camera enable cinematic camera positioning for screenshots
Screenshot command captures viewport images for LM Studio visual verification

nodes.name: School_6_Unreal_Craft_School - MCP Geometry Tools
principles: control_actor spawn_actor creates actors in the world with specified transforms
add_component attaches StaticMeshComponents to actors for geometry placement
set_transform controls position, rotation, and scale of spawned actors precisely
manage_asset create/import handles asset creation and file import workflows

nodes.name: School_6_Unreal_Craft_School - Basic Shape Creation
principles: Primitive shapes (box, sphere, cylinder, cone) serve as foundation geometry for complex meshes
Scale and transform primitives creates varied proportions while maintaining clean topology
Multiple primitives combined via boolean operations create complex architectural forms
Grid snapping ensures consistent placement and modular alignment

nodes.name: School_6_Unreal_Craft_School - Sculpting Workflow
principles: Sculpt brushes (grab, pinch, smooth) enable organic shape manipulation on mesh surfaces
Brush size and strength control the scale and subtlety of sculpted details
Layer-based sculpting preserves non-destructive editing capability
Decimation reduces polygon count while preserving sculpted silhouette for game optimization

nodes.name: School_6_Unreal_Craft_School - Material Application
principles: Materials assigned to geometry via material slots in static mesh editor
PBR material parameters (roughness, metallic, base color) control surface appearance
Material instances allow variation without duplicating full material graphs
UV mapping ensures textures project correctly onto geometry surfaces

nodes.name: School_7_Spatial_Reasoning_School - Spatial Composition
principles: Objects compose in three dimensions - position relative to origin, neighbors, and sight lines matter
Balance achieved through mass distribution: heavy objects low and centered; light objects high and offset
Object placement creates visual paths that guide the eye through 3D space
Depth perception enhanced by overlapping elements and atmospheric perspective (fog distance)

nodes.name: School_7_Spatial_Reasoning_School - Grid Systems
principles: Modular grid (typically 64cm/2ft increments) enables consistent architectural composition
Grid snapping ensures props align with structural elements for believable placement
Multiple grid layers (structural, furnishing, clutter) create organized complexity
Consistent grid usage across all assets enables seamless modular assembly

nodes.name: School_7_Spatial_Reasoning_School - Distance and Scale
principles: Human-scale references establish believable proportions: door ~2m, chair ~0.9m, table ~0.75m
Corridor width 1.2-1.5m for single person; 2-3m for two-person passage
Ceiling height 2.4m (intimate) to 4m (grand) affects emotional perception of space
Debris density correlates with narrative: sparse = abandoned; dense = active/chaotic

nodes.name: School_7_Spatial_Reasoning_School - Spatial Relationships
principles: Every object should have a reason for its position relative to other elements
Light placement follows functional logic: work areas lit, corridors dimmer, corners darkest
Occlusion relationships create depth: foreground objects partially block background
The graph records spatial context - query it before placing any new element

nodes.name: School_8_Iteration_School - Michelangelo Procedure
principles: Rough-cut the form first: establish large shapes and proportions before details
Refine second pass: adjust relationships between elements and improve proportions
Detail third pass: add surface texture, wear patterns, and small props
Polish final pass: lighting adjustments, color correction, atmospheric effects
Each pass removes less but makes more difference - diminishing returns increase with each iteration

nodes.name: School_8_Iteration_School - Iteration Principles
principles: Start with biggest, most obvious elements first (walls, floors, major props)
Verify against reference before moving to details - catch errors early when cheap to fix
Each pass should be smaller and more precise than the last
Stop when further changes do not improve LM Studio assessment score

nodes.name: School_8_Iteration_School - Knowing When to Stop
principles: Goal is not exact match but capturing essence: feeling, principles, truth of the reference
If 10 iterations produce no improvement, return to research for new references or principles
Human feedback overrides objective analysis - if human says it feels wrong, it is wrong

nodes.name: School_8_Iteration_School - Failure Protocol
principles: After 10 failed iterations: return to research, find new references
Return to education: identify missing fundamental principle
Ask the human: show reference and best attempt, ask what they see that is different
Never iterate randomly - every change driven by specific observation or principle

nodes.name: School_9_Emotion_to_Parameter_School - Emotional Lighting
principles: Lonely = single light source + cool temperature (4500K+) + high contrast shadows
Safe = multiple warm sources (3200K) + soft shadows + low contrast
Danger = flickering light + harsh shadows + scorched material palette
Awe = bright directional light (5500K) + dramatic shadows + rich detail surfaces
Mystery = dim colored lighting + deep shadows + obscured materials
Hope = single warm light source in darkness + high contrast worn-but-cared-for materials

nodes.name: School_9_Emotion_to_Parameter_School - Emotional Materials
principles: Rough surfaces = rustic/old/dangerous feeling; smooth surfaces = clean/new/safe
Warm materials (wood, fabric) = comfort and intimacy
Cold materials (metal, glass) = sterile or imposing depending on context
Worn but maintained surfaces suggest hope and resilience in harsh environments

nodes.name: School_9_Emotion_to_Parameter_School - Emotional Sound
principles: Low frequencies create tension, power, dread - use for danger and awe scenes
High frequencies create alertness, anxiety, beauty - use for mystery and hope
Silence creates loneliness, peace, or terror depending on visual context
Steady ambient hum = safety and normalcy; irregular sounds = tension and uncertainty

nodes.name: School_9_Emotion_to_Parameter_School - Emotional Space
principles: Low ceilings (2.4m) = oppressive/intimate/cozy depending on lighting quality
High ceilings (4m+) = freedom/awe or isolation depending on content
Narrow corridors create tension; open spaces create safety or vulnerability
Threshold transitions (narrow to wide) amplify emotional impact of revealed space

nodes.name: School_10_Reference_Management_School - Organization System
principles: Every reference gets unique ID, source URL, date collected, category, subject, emotional tags
Store in Graphify as Reference nodes linked to Pattern nodes and Education nodes
Folder structure: research/[category]/[subject]/ with images, descriptions, extracted parameters

nodes.name: School_10_Reference_Management_School - Avoiding Duplication
principles: Before new research, query Graphify for existing patterns on same subject
If patterns exist, start from those - only research new aspects
Never re-research the same thing unless previous research failed verification

nodes.name: School_10_Reference_Management_School - Cross-Referencing
principles: Study related domains: naval ship lighting informs station lighting; hospital lighting informs habitat lighting
Link related references across categories - graph shows connections humans miss
Principles transfer across domains: same composition rules apply to space stations and cathedrals

nodes.name: School_10_Reference_Management_School - Reference Decay
principles: References age - patterns extracted months ago may be superseded by better understanding
Periodically re-verify old patterns against new references
Mark patterns as superseded rather than deleting them - history matters for learning

nodes.name: School_11_Creativity_School - Combinatorial Creativity
principles: Nothing is truly original - everything is a remix of existing references
The art is in which references you combine and how you transform them
Combine principles from unrelated domains: Gothic cathedral architecture + zero-G physics

nodes.name: School_11_Creativity_School - Extrapolation
principles: Take a principle from one domain and apply it to another unexpectedly
Ask what-if questions: what if a space station had cathedral proportions?
Extrapolate real-world constraints into future contexts with imagination

nodes.name: School_11_Creativity_School - Constraints as Creativity
principles: DSL defines constraints - these are not limitations but the frame that makes painting possible
Engine limits (polygon count, draw calls) force creative optimization solutions
Creative constraints produce more focused and intentional design decisions

nodes.name: School_11_Creativity_School - Idea Log
principles: Save ideas that do not fit current task as Idea nodes in Graphify
Ideas can be combined later - the graph grows with what could be, not just what is
Review idea log periodically for unexpected connections and opportunities

nodes.name: School_12_Collaboration_School - Presenting Options
principles: When multiple approaches exist, present them clearly to the human with pros/cons
Never assume you know what the human wants - show options and let them choose
Visual comparisons (screenshots) are more effective than textual descriptions

nodes.name: School_12_Collaboration_School - Asking for Guidance
principles: When stuck after multiple iterations, ask directly: I have tried X, Y, Z. Do you see something missing?
The human sees things the AI does not - they hold the vision
Frame questions specifically: what emotion is wrong? what proportion feels off?

nodes.name: School_12_Collaboration_School - Incorporating Feedback
principles: Record all human feedback in Graphify and link to relevant patterns
Human feedback overrides objective analysis when conflicts arise
If LM Studio says it matches but human says it feels wrong - the human is right. Research why.

nodes.name: School_12_Collaboration_School - Mirror Protocol
principles: Job is to reflect the human vision back with clarity, not impose own aesthetic
Show work honestly and ask if it matches what they imagined
If it does not match, that is not failure - it is the next iteration. The mirror gets clearer each reflection.

nodes.name: School_13_Record_Education - Complete Education Record
principles: All principles from all schools should be linked to relevant Feature Ledger entries
Cross-reference related principles across disciplines for richer understanding
Education is never complete - new references and insights continuously enrich the graph
The tree grows with every lesson. The mirror sharpens with every insight.
